Reformed Confessions
ri-FORMD kuhn-FESH-uhnz
doctrinal phrase
From Reformed and confessions (Latin confessio, a public acknowledgment of faith); the doctrinal standards of the Reformed churches.

Biblical Definition

The Reformed confessions are the doctrinal standards by which the Reformed churches have publicly confessed their faith—corporate, ordered statements of what the church believes the Scriptures to teach, framed to confess the truth, exclude error, instruct the people, and bind the church’s teachers. They are subordinate standards, always beneath Scripture and answerable to it, yet binding upon those churches that receive them. The chief among them include, in the Continental tradition, the Three Forms of Unity—the Belgic Confession, the Heidelberg Catechism, and the Canons of Dort; the Second Helvetic Confession; and in the British tradition the Westminster Confession of Faith with its Larger and Shorter Catechisms, and, for the Reformed Baptists, the 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith, which largely follows Westminster except on baptism, the church, and the civil magistrate. These confessions arose in the heat of the Reformation and the controversies that followed, hammered out by assemblies of godly and learned men to set forth the recovered gospel of grace with clarity and to guard it against Rome, against Arminianism, and against every error. The dictionary honors the Reformed confessions as faithful summaries of biblical truth and precious instruments of the church’s unity, teaching, and stability, while always holding them in their proper place: they bind the conscience only as they agree with Scripture, which alone is the supreme and infallible rule, and they are honored not as a rival to the Word but as the church’s ordered confession of what the Word teaches.

Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrinal standards of the Reformed churches—Belgic, Heidelberg, Dort, Westminster, the 1689, and others—subordinate to Scripture yet binding on the churches that receive them.

REFORMED CONFESSIONS, the doctrinal standards of the Reformed churches.

Ordered public statements of what the church believes Scripture teaches.

Subordinate to Scripture, yet binding on the churches that receive them.

Include the Three Forms of Unity, Westminster, and the 1689 Baptist Confession.

Framed to confess truth, exclude error, instruct the people, and bind teachers.

Key Scripture

2Ti 1:13 — "Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus."

Rom 10:10 — "For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation."

Jud 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

1Ti 6:12 — "Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses."

Modern Corruption

Confessions are either exalted above Scripture or despised as needless, against their proper place as subordinate standards.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the right place of confessions: subordinate to Scripture, yet binding on the churches that receive them. An anti-creedal spirit, common in the age, despises all confessions as needless human additions and boasts “no creed but the Bible”—forgetting that everyone has a confession, whether written and accountable or unwritten and hidden, and that the church is commanded to hold fast the form of sound words and to confess the faith with the mouth.

The opposite error exalts the confession to the place of Scripture, treating the standard as itself infallible and binding the conscience absolutely. The dictionary holds the Reformed balance. The confessions are faithful summaries of biblical truth, precious for unity, teaching, and stability, and rightly binding on the churches that adopt them and the teachers who subscribe them; but they are subordinate standards, beneath the Word and answerable to it, binding the conscience only as they agree with Scripture, which alone is the supreme and infallible rule of faith and life. They are the church’s ordered confession of what the Word teaches, not a rival to the Word itself.

Hebrew Roots

The phrase names the Reformed churches’ doctrinal standards—subordinate confessions of the faith taught in Scripture.

expand to see more

Latin confessio — a public acknowledgment or profession of faith.

The Three Forms of Unity — Belgic, Heidelberg, and Dort.

The Westminster Standards — Confession, Larger and Shorter Catechisms.

The 1689 London Baptist Confession — the Reformed Baptist standard.

Subordinate standards: binding for the church, yet beneath Scripture.

Usage

"The Reformed confessions are cited as the doctrinal standards of the Reformed churches."

"They are held as subordinate to Scripture against both exalting and despising them."

"“No creed but the Bible” is answered by the duty to confess the faith."
